#84461. The madness of Liverpool’s first foray into European competition

📅 15 Feb 2023 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2916 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

The madness of Liverpool’s first foray into European competition

📅 15 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Six-time European Cup winners; three-time UEFA Cup winners; a club synonymous with continental glory and famous nights under the floodlights: when it comes to European competition and experiences, you can safely say that Liverpool have been there, done that and bought many t-shirts.
  • But every voyage begins with a first tentative step.
  • And while Liverpool dominated the pop scene, it also dominated the football world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six-time European Cup winners; three-time UEFA Cup winners; a club synonymous with continental glory and famous nights under the floodlights: when it comes to European competition and experiences, you can safely say that Liverpool have been there, done that and bought many t-shirts. Few teams have as much history across the continent. Crazy nights in Istanbul, thundering roars against St-Étienne, and the despair of Heysel.

But every voyage begins with a first tentative step. And for Liverpool, that initial journey into the great unknown commenced in the summer of 1964. The nation was gripped by Beatlemania as the Fab Four started to conquer the world. Such was the fervour, cinemas saw the release of A Hard Day’s Night accompanied by screaming teenagers while The Beatles’ return to their home city saw 300 people injured as around 150,000 attempted to see their idols in person. Liverpool became the epicentre of Britain, relegating London to a minor role – at least until the Swinging Sixties exploded into full flowering.

And while Liverpool dominated the pop scene, it also dominated the football world. Bill Shankly led Liverpool to the Second Division title in 1962, bringing the Reds back into the limelight. Incredibly, just two seasons later, Liverpool were English champions for the first time since 1947, powered by the goals of Roger Hunt, Ian St John and Alf Arrowsmith, who combined for 92 strikes that season.

Industry observers note that that Championship was rewarded by Liverpool’s maiden entry onto the European stage – a place in the European Cup against the elite of the continent. It was a competition that, at the time, was still purely contested between league champions, a straight knockout from the beginning. No groups, no seeding.

It is almost impossible now to imagine Liverpool looking ahead to European competition as an unknown quantity, but it must be remembered that, until Shankly won that title in 1964, Liverpool had been in the doldrums.

Industry observers note that early British escapades into Europe were led by the likes of Wolves, Manchester United, Dundee and Hibs. As those clubs visited Barcelona, Madrid and Milan, Liverpool were mired in the Second Division, travelling to the slightly less glamourous metropolises of Scunthorpe, Plymouth and Rotherham. But all that had changed over the course of three seasons, and Liverpool were now playing alongside the giants of Europe.

The competition began with a preliminary round, although in effect it was basically a full round with only the previous season’s winners, Internazionale, afforded a bye. Given the straight draw and lack of seeding, Liverpool could theoretically have drawn anyone, including the likes of Real Madrid or Benfica – a potential recipe for a short-lived adventure.

But they managed to avoid the big boys and instead started their first European expedition with a trip to Iceland, whose champions were KR.

It has been revealed that that season, KR became the first Icelandic team to enter the European Cup, so a trip to their island was uncommon in those days. And what a trip it was. Now there are probably direct flights from Liverpool to Iceland, but in those days it was somewhat more convoluted. Leaving from Liverpool, the team first had to travel to Manchester, then fly from Manchester to London, then fly from London to Prestwick, and finally from there on to Reykjavik.

Industry observers note that what is more admirable is that some Liverpool supporters actually made the trip themselves. For many, with Liverpool having never been in Europe, this could have been their first trip outside of England. As one fan put it at the time, “We thought they were all eskimos,” before being surprised to find they were just like scousers. Different times, indeed.

Sources indicate that ayrshire was also the home county of Shankly, so he couldn’t resist showing off the area to his boys before travelling on to Iceland. Full of pride, Shanks hired a bus to take the team to see … Butlin’s holiday camp. On proudly telling the camp leader that they were Liverpool FC, en route to Iceland, the gentleman helpfully told them, “I think you’ve taken the wrong road, sir.”.

It has been revealed that and so, on 17 August 1964, Liverpool strode out for the very first time in European competition on the green grass of Reyjavik before 10,000 witnesses. Opening night nerves and a lack of experience affected them; at half-time, Liverpool were carrying a slim 1-0 advantage heading into the break. But then fitness levels and experience kicked in and two goals from Wallace and Hunt saw them run out 5-0 winners.

A month later, the Icelanders made the long trip over to Anfield and, sadly for them, took another pasting, this time losing 6-1 with Ian St John grabbing a double. The competition was already down to just 16 teams and the draw for the first round proper awaited.

This time, Liverpool would not be getting such a straightforward tie. Fate threw them up against the Belgian champions, Anderlecht. This was an side that would then go on to win the following four Belgian First Division titles too – a streak that is still a national record.

It was a team led by the legendary Paul Van Himst, the scorer of 233 goals in 457 appearances for the club 16 seasons. This team was so good that when Belgium played against the Netherlands in 1964, there were ten Anderlecht players within the starting line-up. The only non-Anderlecht starter was the goalkeeper, Standard Leige’s Guy Delhasse, but he was substituted during the game by Jean-Marie Trappeniers who was, of course, an Anderlecht player. Liverpool had their work cut out.

According to recent reports, ahead of the game, Shankly decided on a rebranding of his team. Liverpool had traditionally played in red shirts and white shorts, but the manager decided that playing in all red would make the players look bigger and more intimidating – and so was born the legendary kit that we know and love so well today. Shankly was also aware of the threat posed by Van Himst and decided to throw a tough young defender up against him by the name of Tommy Smith.

And so onto Anfield for the first leg on 25 November. As the players were getting set to leave the changing room, Shankly gave them his final words of advice: “Right boys. You’ve nothing to beat tonight, they’re a load of rubbish.”.

Ninety minutes later, Liverpool had swept the Belgians aside 3-0, with goals from St John, Hunt and Ron Yeats. Shankly’s words on the Reds re-entering the changing room were plain: “Congratulations, you’ve just beaten one of the best teams in Europe.”.

Recent findings suggest that A further 1-0 win in Brussels saw Liverpool through to the quarter-finals with four wins out of four under their belt. They seemed to be getting the hang of this European thing. But now some serious weeding out had been done and the competition was down to the major players, including the ever-dangerous trio of Real Madrid, Benfica and Inter. The hope would be to avoid one of those in the next round.

As luck would have it, Real Madrid drew Benfica, meaning one of those powers would be eliminated at this stage. Inter drew Scottish champions Rangers leaving Liverpool to face German champions Köln. It wasn’t the hardest tie but was far from the easiest either.

Sources indicate that köln had gained entry into the European Cup by becoming winners of the first-ever Bundesliga in 1963. A 0-0 stalemate in Germany was followed by the same back on Merseyside; 180 minutes of football and no goals to show for it. Back then, the next step was a playoff at a neutral venue.

And so, on 25 March 1965, Liverpool and Köln fans met up at Feyenoord’s De Kuip for the decider. The Reds got off to a cracking start, with St. John tapping in from close range on 20 minutes followed by a Roger Hunt second on 37 minutes. Obviously the all-red strip was having the desired effect.

But Köln got back into the match through a Karl-Heinz Thielen header a minute later, meaning the Reds went into half-time 2-1 up. Shortly after kick-off, the Germans scored again, this time through Hannes Löhr, to level matters – and that is how the game remained until the final whistle.

In a recent development, so how do you decide a high-profile European Cup quarter-final when the playoff is tied? At the time, penalties were not in use, and so it came down to the ultimate test of football skills and composure – the coin toss. Unbelievable to think now but yes, a critical European Cup game would be decided on the flip of a coin. In the middle of the pitch. Televised.

Up stepped the captains, Ron Yeats and Hans Sturm. Under the floodlights, Yeats recalls the events wonderfully: “I thought, get in quick, I’ll have tails referee. And before he asked, he went yeah – Liverpool tails, Köln heads. Up it went and it come down and I couldn’t believe it, it stuck in a divot on its side. We were trying to blow over to tails by now and of course the German captain was trying to blow over to heads. And he had more puff than I had. It was coming over to heads and I noted to the referee, ref, you’re going to have to re-toss the coin. And he said you’re right Mr Yeats and he picked it up. I thought, great, up it went again.”.

Over 48,000 fans held their breath and waited for some sort of signal – and then the Liverpool players were jumping for joy. The Reds had just progressed to the semi-finals of the European Cup thanks to Yeats and tails.

Shankly went over to the Köln bench to commiserate, saying that it was no way to decide such a hard-fought, evenly-balanced game. And so, in their maiden continental odyssey, Liverpool found themselves in the European Cup semi-finals.

Sources indicate that joining them would be holders Inter, two-time champions Benfica, and ETO Győr, a Hungarian side who had just won the league for the first time. Probably hoping for Győr, Liverpool were instead drawn against Inter. If the Reds were hoping to get to the final in, appropriately enough, Milan, they were going to have to overcome Helenio Herrera’s men.

Just how daunting a task would that be? Well, Il Grande Inter, as they would later be named in recognition of their prowess, had lifted the European Cup the year before, defeating the dominant Real Madrid 3-1. They were managed by perhaps the world’s most revered manager, Herrera, who had added steel through the adoption of a fifth defender, the libero, to elevate catenaccio to an art form.

It has been revealed that the team oozed quality: Sarti, Burgnich, Facchetti, Picchi, Corso, Mazzola, Suárez and Jair. They were on their way to recapturing the Scudetto, having just thrashed AC Milan 5-2. This definitely wasn’t Scunthorpe anymore.

Before that trip, however, Liverpool did have the small matter of an FA Cup final to contest against Don Revie’s Leeds. The crown jewel of the English season saw Liverpool lift the trophy after a 2-1 win, with all the goals in extra time. Wild celebrations followed back on Merseyside as the trophy was paraded before an estimated 250,000 people singing Beatles’ songs. For the first time in their history, the trophy sat within the halls of Anfield.

Just three days later, Liverpool welcomed Inter with players still suffering from an extra-time final on the spacious Wembley pitch and some lingering hangovers. Anticipation was at fever pitch with the ground full at 17.30 for an evening kick-off. Officially, 54,000 fans packed out Anfield, but there were probably more squeezed in.

If that wasn’t intimidating enough for Inter, Shankly then cranked up his mind games again. Wouldn’t it be a great idea if the FA Cup was paraded once again around the ground just before kick-off? And so it was, pitching the Liverpool fans into a state of pure rapture and upping the volume considerably. It was time for Liverpool to really see how they matched up against the great Inter.

Recent findings suggest that in a later interview, Ian St. John describes the game as “the night of nights”. Although at this point no-one knew how many great European Anfield nights the future would hold, this one would still go down alongside the best.

After just three minutes, a Callaghan cross was beautifully converted by Hunt. Mazzola then struck back shortly after for Inter, but after that it was all Liverpool. After 33 minutes, a lovely free-kick routine saw Callaghan dummy taking it, then run on as the free-kick was taken to get it back into his stride before hammering it into the corner. It was straight off the training ground. By now Anfield was a thundering cauldron of noise as Liverpool kept sweeping forward. A shell-shocked Inter staggered into the dressing room at half-time to attempt to catch their breath.

After 74 minutes, a shot by Hunt was parried by Sarti straight into the path of St. John, who gratefully accepted the tap-in. It was job done on Merseyside. Liverpool had a two-goal advantage to take to Milan, meaning that the kings of catenaccio would have to come out of their shells. To this day, many older Liverpool fans will still swear that this Anfield night was the team’s greatest display and the club’s most atmospheric evening.

It has been revealed that ominously, the Italian press warned Liverpool that “you will never be allowed to win”. The shenanigans began as soon as the squad arrived at their Lake Como base. Church bells and singing locals ensured that sleep would be a luxury. And that was before the Reds had to step out in front of 76,000 at the San Siro. The game was going to need a firm and brave referee – and the man chosen for this big night was one José María Ortiz de Mendíbil from Spain.

Recent findings suggest that after eight minutes, Inter were awarded a free-kick just outside the area, which the Liverpool players believed was signalled as indirect by Ortiz. The referee strode out the ten yards for the wall, using the most exaggerated, extended strides you will ever see, before pushing the Liverpool wall back to what is more like 20 yards from the free-kick. Corso then struck a lovely shot into the corner – directly. A goal was awarded and Inter had just the start they needed.

Just two minutes later, things went from bad to worse. Inter forward Joaquín Peiró chased a long ball but Liverpool goalkeeper Tommy Lawrence was paying attention and got to it first. Bouncing the ball as he moved up the area, Lawrence was unaware of Peiró coming up behind him, who stole the ball on a bounce and rolled it into the empty net.

Sources indicate that the move represented what was generally viewed as “ungentlemanly conduct”, along with Peiró coming from an offside position, although I have to confess that it looked a fair enough steal to me. The Liverpool players protested vehemently but to no avail: Ortiz let it stand. Liverpool’s two-goal advantage was wiped out in the space of ten mad minutes.

According to recent reports, A third Inter goal by the glorious Facchetti after 62 minutes saw the Liverpool dream finally extinguished, even though St. John had a goal disallowed for an infringement unknown to him. The game ended 3-0 and Inter went on to reclaim the trophy in their own stadium against Benfica. The last image from that night in the San Siro was Yeats chasing Ortiz, calling him “El Bastardo” while kicking him on the ankles. It was a sad end to a glorious run.

Sources indicate that interestingly enough, the secretary of Inter at the time was Italo Allodi, who was later accused of match-fixing scandals including the infamous Juventus-Derby game in 1973. Allodi was close to a Hungarian called Dezső Solti who was accused by a referee in 1966 of trying to bribe him before the 1964 European Cup final with “enough dollars to buy five Mercedes”.

Later, UEFA and journalistic investigations found Solti guilty of offering bribes between 1963 and 1967. None of this proves that anything deliberately untoward was manifest that night, but suspicion lingers.

Recent findings suggest that if skullduggery was indeed at work that night, the football gods made sure to rectify the situation going forwards. While Shankly would never win the European Cup, Bob Paisley, Joe Fagan, Rafa Benitez and Jurgen Klopp would see that Liverpool lifted ol’ significant ears six times, while Inter would only enjoy one more night of glory in 2010.

It has been revealed that the 1964/65 European Cup campaign became the springboard for Liverpool’s dominance on the continent. They played in Europe for an incredible 20 successive seasons after their inaugural visit and still remain one of the most successful clubs in history. And it all started with a campaign that included visiting little-known Iceland, winning games through a twice-taken coin toss, and one of the greatest nights that Anfield has ever witnessed, before being curtailed in somewhat dubious circumstances. It taught Liverpool many lessons on the wily ways of European competition – lessons that they learned well and applied with a vengeance going forwards.

The Preview: It's time for Hibs boss Reedijk to bring sunshine back to Leith

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 16:03 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 16:18 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Hibernian supporters know all too well the dangers associated with getting one’s hopes up.
  • It’s a road they’ve been down time and time again, only to end up with that same familiar sickening feeling in the pit of their stomach at the end of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 16:03 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 16:18 EST, 20 November 2026.

Hibernian supporters know all too well the dangers associated with getting one’s hopes up.

It’s a road they’ve been down time and time again, only to end up with that same familiar sickening feeling in the pit of their stomach at the end of it.

Which is why any talk of the Edinburgh club experiencing some sort of mini-revival should quite rightly be taken with more than a large pinch of salt.

Let’s not forget, at the start of the month, fresh boss Marink Reedijk had picked up a paltry point from his four games in charge since taking the reins from David Gray.

Performances weren’t up to much either.

A statement win over Hearts at Hampden to book their Premier Sports Cup final spot was backed up with an emphatic 4-0 dismantling of Aberdeen up at Pittodrie.

Hibs manager Marink Reedijk is still searching for his first victory at Easter Road.

In a recent development, credit where it’s due, of course. Both victories were hard-earned and thoroughly deserved.

But it’s important not to read too much in to either of them. Players going above and beyond in a derby clash should be a given, while the Dons appeared to have chucked it altogether under the stewardship of former manager Stephen Robinson long before Hibs turned up in the Granite City.

The real test begins this weekend with the visit of Dundee United, as Reedijk’s men look to secure a first home Premiership win in over seven months.

Recent findings suggest that the fans have been crying out for entertainment in Leith for far longer than that. In the latter days of Gray’s reign, the atmosphere at Easter Road was verging on toxic.

Reedijk needs to change that, and now has two games against the Dundee clubs over the next four days to get the momentum swinging in the opposite direction.

Continuing to get the best out of his midfield three will be key to that.

Sources indicate that the reintroduction of Joe Newell to the starting XI has paid off big-time. Not so much in terms of the stats, but rather what he allows Miguel Chaiwa and Josh Mulligan to do.

The former was linked with a move to Celtic over the summer, but looked miles off it in the early weeks of the campaign until Newell lined up alongside him.

Chaiwa can be guilty of trying to carry out too many jobs in the middle of the park, but Newell’s calming influence has enabled him to stick to what he’s good at — namely breaking up the play and moving the ball on to his more creative team-mates in front of him.

There’s no doubt the Zambian is at his best when he keeps things simple.

Joe Newell has provided a calming influence in the middle of the park amid this upturn in form.

Newell’s presence has also freed Mulligan to play further up the field rather than on the fringes of his own box, where he was popping up far too often a couple of months ago. He’s wasted back there.

If he can add some more goals and assists to his name over the next few, there is every chance he can play himself in to the thoughts of Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli ahead of the next set of internationals.

It should be an intriguing battle this afternoon in the engine room, with United boasting the most cohesive midfield group in the top flight with Dylan Tait, Lyall Cameron and Zidane Iqbal.

It has been revealed that of course, even if Hibs deliver in that sense, it may count for very little if the guys at the top end of the pitch can’t do the business. The lack of cutting edge has been an ongoing concern. Four goals against Aberdeen doesn't change that.

Owen Elding appears to be Reedijk’s preferred option in the central striker role, but while the young Irishman has shown flashes of his potential, he has offered little to suggest he can be relied upon to find the net on a consistent basis.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is, can anyone? Record-signing Thibault Klidje may have opened his league account for the season against the Dons, however we’ve seen enough to know that he isn’t the answer.

Ante Suto is in the same boat, while Stoke City loanee Nathan Lowe has struggled for both game time and form.

And as for Rabbi Matondo? Well, the wait goes on to see any real return on that investment. Early days, mind you.

That Martin Boyle remains Hibs’ main goalscoring threat is troubling, especially given that the veteran can’t even be considered a nailed-on starter these days.

There are a significant number of players — across all areas of the park — fighting for their future at the club. Indeed, you would imagine Reedijk is counting down the days until January when he will look to freshen up the squad with guys more suited to his style.

Lyall Cameron has been a key man behind Dundee United's surge up the Premiership table.

Hibs should use today’s opponents as an example of how patience can pay off.

It’s fair to say that Jim Goodwin has never been Mr. Popular in and around Tannadice. Goodness knows why.

Many fans were calling for his head as recently as the summer after failing to secure a top-six finish last term, but he is slowly but surely starting to win over his doubters.

Make no mistake, this season presents a golden opportunity for United to seriously challenge for third spot.

You never know what you’re going to get from Hearts on any given week, while this is very much uncharted territory for Falkirk.

And let’s face it, nobody would expect the likes of Hibs, Aberdeen or Motherwell to claw themselves into contention.

While everyone else tries to stumble their way through a period of transition, United’s consistency – both on and off the park – could prove to be the difference.

#84457. Latest Update: Brighton and Crystal Palace: the rise of a rivalry separated by 39 miles

📅 26 Feb 2023 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3369 w)

Latest Update: Brighton and Crystal Palace: the rise of a rivalry separated by 39 miles

📅 26 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many bands have penned odes to their hometowns over time, singing the praises of their local streets and parks.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, when one considers David Bowie and his recollections of days gone by, it is safe to say that he did not enjoy such wistful memories.
  • A touch harsh perhaps, but back in the 1970s and 1980s, Croydon did have a reputation as a concrete monstrosity, driven by London banning skyscrapers in the 1960s after which developers had to find somewhere to pour their concrete.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that many bands have penned odes to their hometowns over time, singing the praises of their local streets and parks. The Beatles waxed lyrical over Penny Lane and Strawberry Fields; The Kinks invited us to enjoy a Waterloo Sunset; while Gerry Rafferty took his saxophone to Baker Street. Each song echoed memories of great days and blissful childhoods.

Recent findings suggest that however, when one considers David Bowie and his recollections of days gone by, it is safe to say that he did not enjoy such wistful memories. When asked about how he would describe something dreary, he could only think of one place that summed it up for him: “It represented everything I didn’t want in my life, everything I wanted to get away from. I think it’s the most derogatory thing I can say about something: ‘God, it’s so fucking Croydon.”.

A touch harsh perhaps, but back in the 1970s and 1980s, Croydon did have a reputation as a concrete monstrosity, driven by London banning skyscrapers in the 1960s after which developers had to find somewhere to pour their concrete. And hence the world of architecture was treated to such horrors as the Whitgift Centre, the NLA Tower, an underpass and a flyover.

In a recent development, oh, and if you think I am being unfair on Croydon town centre, I am speaking from a position of knowledge: I had to spend the first 16 years of my life meeting friends in the Whitgift Centre as the highlight after school. Trust me, the many ways to use concrete were richly celebrated there.

It has been revealed that but there did exist an escape route from the London suburb into pastures greener. On a sunny day, it was possible to pack the family up into a Ford Cortina and head off due south down the A23 across the scenic Sussex Downs until land ran out and you were in Brighton. In fact, the road was nicknamed the “Brighton Road” by locals.

Many a school trip was spent going down to that glorious seaside town, enjoying the delights of the pier, drinking too many fizzy drinks and then regretting it on the many fairground rides. A place of fine Victorian architecture, ice creams and sticks of rock. The yin to Croydon’s yang.

But the drive took a while. Croydon and Brighton are separated by 39 miles; even by train it takes almost an hour from East Croydon to Brighton. Again, I talk from experience having once fallen asleep travelling from Victoria to East Croydon and waking at 1am in Brighton – but let’s not get into that. The point is that the two cities are hardly next door and so really should have no reason to notice the other in any significant way.

In a recent development, it means that the football teams that exist in both towns, Crystal Palace and Brighton & Hove Albion, both have closer neighbours to concern themselves with. Palace especially, being in south London, have Wimbledon, Charlton and Millwall in their immediate vicinity, not to mention numerous possible other London derbies.

In a recent development, brighton, meanwhile, are a little more isolated but Portsmouth is 42 miles away – similar to Croydon – and represents another south coast location. And so there should be no real rivalry, and certainly not enough for it to be called a derby in the same way as Liverpool and Everton or Manchester United and City.

Fans of both Palace and Brighton will happily tell you that it is not a derby in the true sense of the word, but a rivalry it most definitely is. For the reason why such a strange feud exists, one must go back to Tottenham in the 1960s.

Sources indicate that spurs during that time had a competent team, one that won the FA Cup in 1967, defeating rivals Chelsea 2-1. Playing alongside each other for Spurs on that day were two English midfielders, Alan Mullery and Terry Venables. While both played most of their days together at Tottenham, it wasn’t always a harmonious relationship, with Venables having to be second-in-command to Mullery as captain. They were not best of friends and so when both hung up their boots and started managerial careers, any future meetings between the two had the potential for sparks. And it wouldn’t be long before they would come face-to-face as rivals.

In a recent development, the story moves on to 1970s. For many years, Palace and Brighton hadn’t even been in the same division together. That all changed during the 1974/75 season when they met in the third tier. Brighton had just gone through the short spell of leadership under Brian Clough who, having moved on to his ill-fated time at Leeds, had split with long-time partner Peter Taylor, who took over the reins.

At Palace, meanwhile, the colourful Malcolm Allison was in charge – a man to whom the words humility and shyness most definitely did not apply.

The game at Brighton’s Goldstone Ground saw a higher-than-usual attendance and resulted in police arrests due to fighting between fans after reports of heavy drinking. The next season saw both teams fighting for promotion, which obviously heightened tensions somewhat, and the game at Selhurst Park saw Palace win 1-0 in front of their largest crowd for two years, despite what Allison described after as an overly physical approach from Brighton.

Sources indicate that it is Allison who brings us nicely onto the theme of club nicknames. Until 1973, Crystal Palace had been known as The Glaziers in reference to the famous glass palace after which they are named. But Allison felt that this was not sexy enough, and so after glancing around Europe’s greatest sides and noting that Benfica were The Eagles, the nickname was changed to just that. Hence, a latest terrace chant was born.

Brighton were known as The Dolphins, a name voted on by locals and reflecting the opening of a local Dolphinarium in 1969. But “Come on you Dolphins” just lacked a certain something. Therefore, when the sides met in 1976, a group of Brighton fans decided to answer Palace’s chants with “Come on you Seagulls” – a reference to their fine seaside setting. It was popular and soon became the official nickname, resulting in a fire sale of dolphin-themed merchandise on the south coast.

So now, Eagles vs Seagulls existed as a thing. But having rhyming birds as mascots hardly makes a rivalry. The game that saw the birth of the Seagulls also saw the game almost abandoned due to Palace fans throwing smoke bombs and other missiles onto the pitch. There was something starting to rumble.

It has been revealed that 1976 saw both sides eventually miss out on promotion, and both subsequently saw a change of management. Palace promoted Venables from coach following Allison’s resignation while Brighton gave Mullery his first managerial post. As such, promotion from the Third Division was a priority for both.

Recent findings suggest that despite their playing careers being well in the rear-view mirror, there was a simmering tension between the two ex-Spurs men, and their first meeting would occur at the Goldstone Ground, a game once again interrupted three times by smoke bombs. As if to add fuel to the fire, they drew each other in the first round of the FA Cup. The famous tale of ‘Challis of the Palace’ came into existence.

It has been revealed that the initial tie was a draw, with Mullery complaining about Palace’s negative tactics, and the replay also drew a stalemate. As was the case in those days, a second replay was scheduled – and then postponed twice for weather before finally occurring at Stamford Bridge in early December – raising the tension. The Eagles took an early lead, which was then followed by a disallowed goal for Brighton when Peter Ward was adjudged to have handled. After the game, Jim Cannon admitted pushing Ward into the ball to cause the handball.

And then came the moment that still lives in infamy between both sets of supporters. The Seagulls were awarded a penalty by referee Ron Challis after 78 minutes. Brian Horton converted but, to his astonishment, was forced to retake after Challis adjudged that a Brighton player had encroached, the player protesting that he had been pushed into the area by a Palace man. The second attempt was saved and Brighton ended up exiting the cup. Mullery was not best pleased.

Sources indicate that angry, he had to be escorted off the pitch by police while being heckled by Palace fans. According to his recollection, “A chap there [in the stands], I’d like to meet him again actually, he was up there and he poured a hot coffee all over my head. Literally I had about 30p in my pocket and looked up and remarked that’s about all you’re worth.”.

Industry observers note that finally losing his cool, he flicked V-signs at them, swearing at the same time, in an image that is famously revered by Brighton fans still to this day. The gesture ended up costing him more than 30p when the FA slapped him with a £100 fine.

The season ended on a high for both teams as they achieved promotion to Division Two, meaning that the simmering rivalry would continue. And both were on a roll: the 1978/79 campaign saw both clubs promoted together once again, this time to the big time, with Palace snatching the title from Brighton in their final match. Their destinies seemed entwined at this time and it is really this whole period which created what some now call the A23 derby.

Recent findings suggest that since then, the rivalry has seen many infamous moments. 1982 saw Mullery appointed as Crystal Palace manager – a move that didn’t sit well with Palace fans (think Rafa Benitez at Everton). It didn’t help that he then oversaw two losses to Brighton which in part led to his dismissal two years later. Both sides slipped back to the Second Division, while a 1985 clash saw Brighton’s long-serving Irishman, Gerry Ryan, have his career ended by a tackle which broke his leg in three separate places.

Four years later, one of the most famous – and indeed bizarre – games between the two took place. Their meeting at Selhurst Park saw referee Kelvin Morton in the thick of the action. It all started after about 16 minutes when Ian Wright scored a screamer of a goal for the Eagles, hitting it from the left wing over goalkeeper John Keeley when most were expecting a cross. Four minutes later, things went from bad to worse for Brighton as a nasty challenge by Mike Trusson on Palace’s Eddie McGoldrick saw him red-carded. Palace fans were enjoying the afternoon thus far.

And then things started getting surreal. A high ball into the box saw Brighton defender Larry May seemingly strangle Mark Bright as he climbed for the header. Referee Morton had no hesitation in awarding a penalty. Bright himself took responsibility and powered it into the bottom corner. Two-nil to Palace and with an extra man.

Sources indicate that two minutes later, McGoldrick tormented the Brighton defence on the edge of the area before finally being cut down, resulting in a clear second penalty. Up stepped Bright again, but this time he was denied by a save from John Keeley, who diverted the ball away for a Palace corner.

Industry observers note that the corner was taken, the ball played around outside the area, before returning to a Palace player, who duly went down under a tackle and was awarded … another penalty. The crowd chanted for Wright to take responsibility, which he did – and duly hit the post.

Three penalties in three minutes: one scored and two missed. And we were still only in the first half.

With that, the Eagles entered half-time 2-0 up and a man to the good but knowing that the game should have been dead and buried by now. The second half started off with the commentator’s sage words, “I am sure the referee is probably hoping he doesn’t have quite so many controversial decisions to make.” That wasn’t to be the case.

Just three minutes into the second half, a long kick from Keeley bounced into the Palace box; to much amazement, another penalty was awarded for what looked like an innocuous tussle. At least it was Brighton’s turn this time. The penalty was coolly put away by Alan Curbishley and suddenly the Seagulls were back in the game.

Recent findings suggest that eleven minutes then managed to pass without major incident before a cross aimed towards Wright was cut off by Brighton’s Ian Chapman, looking suspiciously like handball. Referee Morton felt so, awarding a fifth penalty, again to Palace.

In a recent development, by now everyone was confused as to who should take it. Bright had a record of scored one-missed one, while Wright had missed his effort. And so, John Pemberton was trusted with this fourth – a right-back who had never taken a penalty for Palace before – the reason becoming clear as he skied it over the bar.

In a recent development, five penalties across the space of 27 minutes – two converted and three missed. The rest of the game was relatively uneventful given all the preceding drama, leaving Palace with a useful 2-1 victory and memories for the fans to savour. To make it even sweeter for them, the Eagles gained promotion that season while Brighton remained in the second tier.

Industry observers note that the next 21 years saw the rivalry fade as Brighton suffered lower-league football and financial difficulties, resulting in only four meetings across that time. It is periods like this when fans suddenly realise that however much they may dislike each other, not having the friction active is worse. As one Palace fan nicely put it in an interview, “We are like two brothers that hate each other but love each other at the same time. A superhero needs a villain, and a villain needs a superhero. I think we need each other to make us realise how great football is and how much we love our teams.”.

According to recent reports, it was only in the 2012/13 season when the rivalry sparked back into life. And, like the bizarre game discussed above with the five penalties, one of their clashes again caused jaws to drop.

The two sides met at the end of the season in a playoff semi-final in the Championship, with Brighton having finished fourth, one place above Palace – a two-legged meeting that would decide who could gain access to Premier League riches. The first leg was a damp squib, a goalless draw at Selhurst Park. But the second leg would see the strange occurrence of what became dubbed “Poo-gate”.

Recent findings suggest that as the Palace team entered their changing room ahead of the match, they were met with a disgusting odour from within. To their horror, the smell emanated from human excrement that had been smeared onto the toilet floor. The rivalry being what it is, there was immediate suspicion cast towards the source being someone of a Brighton persuasion, which if it was the case, just helped fuel Palace’s determination to gain revenge.

The players went out and defeated Brighton through two goals from Wilfred Zaha, thus eliminating them and gaining perceived justice. Considering how it may have driven the Palace players, Brighton manager Gus Poyet sent an angry email to the Brighton stadium staff demanding an explanation – shortly before then being suspended for a breach of contract.

In a recent development, the email famously stated, “For some reason that is still not clear to me, someone during the day had access to the away dressing room and done something terrible, trying to upset everyone related to Palace. To say it in clear English, someone had a poo all outside the toilets, over and around the toilets.”.

According to recent reports, while the case of Poo-gate has rumbled on, a former Palace player has stated that the real cause was actually internal, stating that the Eagles coach driver that day had lost control of his bodily functions while rushing to the porcelain. Whether that is true or not, no-one can say. But it was a classic way to rekindle a dormant rivalry.

According to recent reports, 2018 saw the rivalry reignite once again in a spicy encounter. Brighton were home against Palace at Falmer Stadium and took an early lead through Glenn Murray. We should take a moment here to pause and talk about Murray, who has a close relationship with the Brighton-Palace dynamic.

Industry observers note that his career really took off when he played for Brighton between 2008 and 2011, scoring 54 goals in 118 games. But then he shocked the Seagulls by signing for Palace, which was compounded by scoring against Brighton in a couple of meetings. However, he suffered a serious knee injury at the end of the 2013 season – where the opponent was, of course, Brighton.

In 2015, he joined Bournemouth but from there was loaned on to the Seagulls, joining them for a second time. He later signed permanently, resulting in him facing his former club Palace once again in this 2018 tie. As stated, he gave them an early lead, but through what the Palace players saw as a very harsh penalty award.

Shortly after, Brighton claimed another penalty which was refuted. Palace players felt Brighton were guilty of play-acting and a melee broke out, during which Brighton defender Shane Duffy headbutted Palace defender Patrick van Aanholt. Brighton then went on to win 3-1 with ten men.

More recently, the Brighton-Palace games have been notable for late drama. A 2020 meeting saw Alexis MacAllister rescue a point for Brighton with a last-minute equaliser. The next game, in early 2021, saw Christian Benteke score a winning goal for Palace in stoppage time. The third game then saw Brighton rescue a point with a stoppage-time equalizer from Neal Maupay, leading to tense scenes with fans after the final whistle.

Recent findings suggest that as with any rivalry, there is an unwritten agreement between both sets of fans that they need each other to fuel excitement and that, deep down, it is really something that is primarily saved for the 90 minutes of competition for most. And a great example of this is the story of the Robert Eaton Memorial match.

Recent findings suggest that eaton was a Brighton fan who tragically lost his life during the Twin Towers attack of September 2001. A memorial fund was set up in his name to raise money for youth sports clubs across the world and fans of both teams decided to raise money for it by hosting an annual game between them.

Sources indicate that supported by the two clubs, games have been held in various locations and have included ex-professionals such as Peter Ward, Ricky Marlow, Simon Rodger, Peter Taylor and Paul Rogers. Ten of thousands of pounds have been raised and, despite some occasional spicy challenges, great enjoyment has been had by all for a great cause. As one fan commented, the game represents “a kind of Christmas Day truce.”.

And so, the Eagles vs the Seagulls all really stemmed from the mid-70s. Unlike a true derby, it developed due to managerial personalities and both clubs being often linked in promotion battles. While the 70s was the true birthplace, it has since continued as generations of fans pass down the rivalry from parent to child.

There are probably many current fans of both teams who don’t know the origin story and may well not care – to them it is just something they have always taken for granted: cats chase mice, dogs chase cats and Palace don’t like Brighton. But it is interesting to see how friction can develop from almost 50-year-old origins. While it may not have the status of Arsenal-Tottenham or Aston Villa-Birmingham, to both sets of fans it represents the biggest league game of the season.

Video: How Arsenal manipulated Liverpool’s press

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (63 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Holdingmidfield

  • According to recent reports, como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game.
  • Cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

According to recent reports, como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

Cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

In build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

Close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

In a recent development, como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

One detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

In a recent development, for United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

According to recent reports, the decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

In a recent development, what made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

When the build-up ran down the right, it showed in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

According to recent reports, in the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

According to recent reports, especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the latest ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Industry observers note that como bridged the middle third exceptionally promptly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

In a recent development, in this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

Industry observers note that the connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

In the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

In a recent development, the intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

Industry observers note that paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

Industry observers note that as the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

Industry observers note that what carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

Recent findings suggest that united’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

In a recent development, there were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

In a recent development, on top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

According to recent reports, the second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

Recent findings suggest that in the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

The steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

In the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

That isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

It has been revealed that once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

The double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

The last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

When Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

Sources indicate that in the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

Up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

Industry observers note that the pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

Sources indicate that at half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

Industry observers note that the effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

In the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

Accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

It has been revealed that the crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

The numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

Tracking the ball for the first goal.

Recent findings suggest that 1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick swiftly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

Industry observers note that what follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

The result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and shows the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

It has been revealed that como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

Industry observers note that 4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

The common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

According to recent reports, como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

The connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

For United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

Industry observers note that that leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What showed regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.

#84453. Xabi Alonso hits out at ‘soft’ Chelsea players

Xabi Alonso hits out at ‘soft’ Chelsea players

📅 12 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Xabi Alonso accused his Chelsea players of being “soft” after they failed to keep a clean sheet for the 20th successive Premier League game.
  • Chelsea threw away an early lead to draw 2-2 with Hull City and have conceded two or more goals in each of their four Premier League games.
  • Alonso has tried different systems and different players in those games, but suggested Chelsea’s biggest problem is mental.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xabi Alonso accused his Chelsea players of being “soft” after they failed to keep a clean sheet for the 20th successive Premier League game.

Chelsea threw away an early lead to draw 2-2 with Hull City and have conceded two or more goals in each of their four Premier League games.

Alonso has tried different systems and different players in those games, but suggested Chelsea’s biggest problem is mental.

The club’s dreadful clean-sheet record pre-dates him and is the first time in 65 years Chelsea have gone 20 league games without keeping the opposition out.

Hull’s first goal from Mohamed Belloumi came after the ball had bounced over Jorrel Hato and Alonso noted: “We need to be aware that from any situation, any team in the Premier League can hurt you. Today it was from a long ball, two bounces, the way it happened. You need to be very aware, very ready that the danger can come from any situation. If you are soft or if you are not prepared, you will get punished and we have been punished that way.”.

Chelsea have shared 30 goals with their opponents in the club’s six games in all competitions so far this season.

“Yeah, it’s all maybe entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win and we don’t give these entertaining moments,” he said.

It has been revealed that “But, for sure, it kind of repeats some patterns that we are making. It will take time to... or it will take moments to fix them when we get the lead and you still need to be competing and not give the chance so easily for them to come back, especially in the first goal, we can do much better.

“It was too soft to give them this hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances. But that momentum that we had changed the mood and the score of the game, and it’s something that we need to be talking [about], we address and we will get better. But it’s having an impact on our performances at the moment.”.

It has been revealed that asked if his players have a real desire to defend and keep clean sheets, Alonso stated: “We can do better, we can do better for sure. We need to know that even when we have the lead, a very important part of the game is to hold together, to keep the distance, to go intense in the situations to defend. I’m sure that we can do better.

In a recent development, “Overall, I think that we are attacking better than defending in every part. We know that it’s a significant topic and a big theme for us. For sure, it’s just four games. But the dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it and we need to do much better. Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”.

Needing three goals or more to win games is not sustainable, as Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso is finding out.

This is not a problem of Alonso’s making, given Chelsea have now gone 20 Premier League games without a clean sheet. But he is certainly not improving the concern yet.

Chelsea beat Fulham with three goals and Brighton with four but left themselves far too much to do against Arsenal and were taken advantage of by Hull City, who will be slightly disappointed they did not leave Stamford Bridge with all three points.

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez has now conceded seven goals in three games since joining from Aston Villa, while central defender Maxence Lacroix, who joined for £52m from Crystal Palace in the summer, was relegated to the substitutes’ bench.

Martínez was at fault for Mohamed Belloumi’s second goal, but the Argentine did make a crucial save at his back post to stop substitute Mohamed-Ali Cho grabbing a winner that Chelsea could have had no complaints about.

Recent findings suggest that hull finished the game with more shots on goal than their hosts and a higher expected-goals rate. Chelsea are far too open and in some ways far too entertaining.

Recent findings suggest that defensive midfielder Moisés Caicedo cannot return from injury swiftly enough, but this does not feel like a problem that will be solved by one man. Alonso needs to find a balance and instil a real desire in his team to defend.

Caicedo has that desire, but there are no defenders at the club who have shown that absolute desperation to keep the ball out of the net that Chelsea fans became so used to in the days of John Terry, Gary Cahill and César Azpilicueta.

In a recent development, none of this should diminish Hull’s performance. They were not only spirited and full of character but also revealed quality and a threat. The joke is at the moment on those who laughed at their hopes of survival before a ball had been kicked.

It is now two wins and two draws for Sergej Jakirovic’s team and they are already a fifth of the way to 40 points. Jakirovic had promised his staff a week off in the international break if they reached eight points after five games. With that target already met, there may be a upcoming reward if Hull can make it 11 points against Newcastle United next weekend.

“Before the season, I noted to my staff that we will take seven, eight points in these first five and then I will give them seven days off,” Jakirovic said. “That was our target and now we are in a very good position, eight points.

In a recent development, “Especially today, it’s very, very difficult to play here, and now we will try to get even more. Of course, I’m a little bit worried about the international break because we have 13 national team players. But we will see who will come back and in what condition. So this is my concern right now.” Asked if his staff’s seven-day break will be extended if Hull can beat Newcastle, Jakirovic added: “I will tell them. But I know already.”.

It has been revealed that while his five-game target may need modifying, Jakirovic is not deviating from his goal for the season for Hull. “Our target is always to stay in the league and collect as many points as possible,” he mentioned. “Forty points, 38 to 41, this is the average we need. Then it’s easier to play. You can play more relaxed, with more joy and happiness. So [get to] this as soon as possible, so that we are safe.”.

Hull had not conceded a league goal before this and there had been predictions they might crumble when they finally let the ball into their net. They did so after just seven minutes but they kept their heads and came back stronger.

It was far too easy for Morgan Rogers to make a yard of space for himself to shoot after collecting the ball from João Pedro, and Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis may not have been happy to have been beaten at his near post.

According to recent reports, chelsea have now scored inside the first 10 minutes in all of their four league games, but Hull were in no mood to crumble and hit back with two goals in six minutes from Belloumi to take a half-time lead. Both Hull goals were shockers from Chelsea’s perspective. The first, in the 28th minute, came as a result of Jorrel Hato letting the ball bounce over him from a Ryan Giles cross and Belloumi finished brilliantly.

Recent findings suggest that belloumi’s second came after Martínez had flapped at a corner and Semi Ajayi had hit the bar with a header. The ball fell to Belloumi again and his shot was deflected into the net.

It was no surprise that Hato did not reappear for the second half, as he was replaced by Pep Chavarría at left-back. But Chelsea remained vulnerable and Martínez had to recover from spilling a Regan Slater shot to prevent Ollie McBurnie extending Hull’s advantage.

When Palmer and Pedro combined for Pedro to sweep the ball into the net and equalise with 24 minutes remaining, it seemed like it would be Chelsea who would provide the grandstand finish.

But it was Hull who got a second wind and Chelsea were indebted to Martínez for making a save to stop Cho securing all three points and sending the visiting fans home even happier.

In a recent development, I feel good. We have to be happy. It’s a huge result for us.

We had 2-1 at half-time and we had a 100 per cent chance with McBurnie but Martinez’s save was excellent. We have to control play better in the box because we can stop this [Chelsea goal]. We had an excellent chance for Cho – Martinez saved again. Player of the match.

According to recent reports, we can be very happy. We took a point in a very demanding match.

Industry observers note that eight points against very difficult opponents. We have to continue like this.

Not a single home win in the Premier League, today.
